title.en: A queen who would not bow

text.en: Here is a riddle from the book: she was a queen who led the fight, with a shining sword in her hand and her son on her back in a cloth band, and she died defending her motherland. The answer is Rani Abbakka of Ullal, whose story is told in this chapter as an illustrated comic.

You solve the riddle and then name other women warriors who contributed to India's struggle for Independence.
The comic opens with Abbakka's ailing mother lamenting that she lies helpless while the Portuguese are a threat. Abbakka tells her not to tire herself with such thoughts. She promises not to rest until she has driven the Portuguese out of the west coast. Abbakka's kingdom is Ullal. She wants the whole-hearted co-operation of her people to make Ullal stronger, secure and free.
Ullal was a vassal state, a state controlled by a more powerful country that must pay money when asked. Ullal had to pay a tribute to the Portuguese, who had captured it, and the Portuguese also traded in spices. Abbakka announced that she would stop paying the tribute and would not sell the Portuguese spices. Her husband, Veera Narsimha of Bangadi, called it a rash decision, meaning an act done without thinking of the consequences. He feared the Portuguese might think he was in league with her, which means in alliance, and that Bangadi might face their wrath, meaning great anger. He wanted to make her change her mind. Abbakka replied that he might be afraid but she refused to be cowed by them.
Veera Narsimha ordered his soldiers to seize her, which means capture her, but such was the spell of the brave queen that not a soldier stirred. They decided to follow their leader. This only strengthened her resolve, which means determination. Abbakka then addressed a meeting of rajas and asked for their support. They felt that they were no match for the Portuguese and advised her not to provoke them. She said she would fight alone, single-handed.
Next day a Portuguese envoy came to remind her that the annual tribute was long overdue. She answered that Ullal was a sovereign country, meaning a country with complete authority over itself, so it paid no tribute and took no orders from the Portuguese. The envoy warned that she would regret her stand. Abbakka ordered merchant ships to be built. In alliance with the Zamorin of Kozhikode she defied the Portuguese, which means openly disobeyed them, and built a hugely profitable trade with Arabia. The Portuguese navy apprehended, meaning arrested, the ships on their return. Her men fought bravely and all ships returned except her commander's. This deeply angered the queen. The commander had held off the enemy while the others escaped, and his ship must have been captured.
The Portuguese replied by attacking, with cannons booming from across the river. Abbakka sought her mother's blessing, saying that the time to avenge, meaning to take revenge for a wrong, had come. Her forces then took the fort of Mangalore. When the news reached the Portuguese Governor of Goa, he reacted sharply, furious that a mere woman had defeated the mighty Portuguese. The Portuguese rallied their forces to attack Ullal. The dauntless, meaning fearless, Abbakka told her soldiers this would be the decisive, or final and effective, war. For four days the battle raged, but Ullal's forces were enough, and the Portuguese retreated in haste, never to trouble Ullal again. Later Abbakka helped Venkatappa Nayak, King of Keladi, to take the fort of Mangalore, and the Portuguese were eventually driven out of Mangalore by Shivappa Nayak, the greatest of the Keladi kings.
Spelling rule: i before e except after c, as in receive and deceive. Words such as seize and sovereign are exceptions. The blanks give: ceiling, believe, thief, achieve, perceive, protein, society, shield, weight and friend. Silent letters are written but not pronounced, such as the w in wrath, k in knowledge, p in pneumonia, h in honour and l in calm. Expressions with laugh: laughing stock means a person everyone laughs at, and last laugh means the final victory after others laughed. You use burst out laughing, laugh until you cry and have a good laugh in your own sentences. Direct and indirect speech: when reporting, the verb shifts back in tense, pronouns change to fit the reporter, and words of time and place change. Rani said, I will make them pay, becomes Rani said that she would make them pay. Commands become requests, advice or instructions, as in The class teacher requested them to turn off the lights when they left.
In Let us listen you complete a bio-table about Rani Gaidinliu, a freedom fighter from Tamenglong, born in January 1915, a Rongmei (Kabui) Naga, who joined the Hereka Movement for revival of Naga tribal religion and self-rule. Check the facts you fill in against the recording. In Let us speak you practise stressing syllables in words such as vassal, successor, rash, league, wrath, seize and resolve, where wrath rhymes with roth, with a silent w, and seize is read seez, not size. In Let us write you write a conversation between two students, Pratap and Tarana, about women who inspire us in India's past and in the present.

In Let us listen you complete a bio-table about Rani Gaidinliu while the teacher speaks, and the transcript at the end of the unit lets you check your answers. She was born on 26 January 1915 in the Tamenglong district, now in Manipur, and belonged to the Rongmei (Kabui) Naga tribe. At the age of 13, in 1927, she joined the Heraka movement, which aimed at reviving the Naga tribal religion and at self-rule. She was arrested in 1932 at the age of 16 and sentenced to life imprisonment, and she was kept in prisons across the Northeast from 1932 to 1947. She was called the Daughter of the Hills, was given the title Rani for her courage, received the Padma Bhushan in 1982, and died on 17 February 1993 at the age of 78.

why.en: A state controlled by a more powerful country that pays tribute.

text.en: Tense or pronoun change?

prompt.en: Describe how Rani Abbakka defended Ullal and what makes her a braveheart.

requiredIdeas.en: She refused to pay tribute to the Portuguese and called Ullal a sovereign country.
She built merchant ships and traded with Arabia in alliance with the Zamorin of Kozhikode.
She faced attacks bravely, took Fort Mangalore and defeated the Portuguese at Ullal after four days of battle.
She was determined, fearless and inspired her soldiers.

commonMisconceptions.en: She paid the tribute every year.
She asked the Portuguese to rule Ullal.

points.en: Rani Abbakka of Ullal refused to pay tribute to the Portuguese.
Her husband thought it was a rash decision, but her soldiers followed her.
She built ships, traded with Arabia and fought the Portuguese bravely.
Ullal won after four days of battle.
Spelling, silent letters and direct and indirect speech are language points of this chapter.
